artifacts.notes:
A LEAD, NOT A SOURCE. Nothing in this project's Sequence transcription was read out of this file; every line was read on the page images and this text layer served only to find the leaves. It corrupts the incipits it prints -- `Fictimee Paschali laudes` for Victimae Paschali laudes, `Vent Sancte Spirttu` for Veni Sancte Spiritus, `Sequence, 0a»ter-Stm&aj?` for the blackletter `Sequence, Easter-Sunday.` -- so a reading taken from it would be composition.

STORAGE. Registered `remote` because this lane may not add tracked payload bytes. The rights case above is affirmative and complete, so an upgrade to `tracked` is available on the 1843 precedent (`artifact.eugene-cummiskey.roman-missal-english-laity.philadelphia-1843.roman-missal-1843-text-6949d12f`) if a searchable text layer for this edition is wanted; the file is 222,340 bytes over 15,282 LF-terminated lines, valid UTF-8, no CR bytes.

THE GOOGLE CENSUS, RUN OVER THE WHOLE 222,340 BYTES ON 2026-08-20, CASE-INSENSITIVE. Absent: 'usage guidelines' 0, 'about this book' 0, 'about google book search' 0, 'books.google' 0, 'do not assume' 0, 'watermark' 0, 'non-commercial' 0, 'attribution' 0, 'creative commons' 0, 'all rights' 0, 'public domain' 0, 'copyright' 0. Present: the page-foot stamp, 'google' 311 times over 38 distinct line spellings and 358 lines, the commonest being 'Digitized by GoOgle' (160), a bare 'Google' (77), 'litized by Google' (48), 'Digitized by G00gle' (10), down through 'Digitized by CjOCK^Ic' and '>y Google'. That is the SAME SHAPE the 1843 audit found in `roman-missal-1843-text-6949d12f` and decided by retaining the stamp: no single stated deletion removes it and a pattern loose enough to catch the tail would delete real text.

THE THEN-CURRENT GUIDANCE SAID THE OPPOSITE, WHICH IS WHY THE CENSUS IS HERE. The superseded guidance/propers-for-agents.md row recorded that "the 1849 Caswall bytes carry Google's front matter as a single contiguous head block, which is the shape the 1843 audit records as admitting the stated-deletion derivative route, unlike the 1861's page-foot stamp". The head-block shape is real, but it belongs to Internet Archive item `lyracatholicaco00caswgoog`, which is the New York 1851 Dunigan reprint and not this book: measured the same day, that file has 'google' on 11 lines, all in lines 1-46, with 'usage guidelines' 1, 'do not assume' 2, 'public domain' 9, 'copyright' 5, and 'digitized by' 0 -- no page-foot stamp at all. The two items are exactly each other's opposite in this respect, and the superseded guidance row attached the wrong shape to the wrong year. The derivative route is available for THAT item and is not needed for THIS one.

IDENTITY. Item LyraCatholica1849, uploaded 2017-10-17 by a private uploader, collections catholictexts, folkscanomy_religion, folkscanomy; 354 page images at 600 ppi; creator 'Catholic Church; Caswall, Edward, 1814-1878'; publisher 'London : J. Burns'; date 1849. NOTE THE SAME METADATA TRAP THE 1843 RECORD RECORDS: the item's `scanner` field says 'Internet Archive HTML5 Uploader 1.6.3', which describes how a private person uploaded the file and not who made the page images. The images are a Google digitisation -- the stamp is at the foot of every page image opened here, leaves n8, n175-n179 and n270-n281 among them -- so this item is a re-upload of Google-scanned pages re-recognised with ABBYY, and a record reading the `scanner` field alone would state the provenance backwards.
artifacts.rights_basis:
THE BOOK. Published at London in 1849. Any work published before 1931 is out of United States copyright; that is the line guidance/missals.md records from Cornell's public-domain chart, and it is written here AS DERIVED FOR CALENDAR YEAR 2026, not as a standing rule -- on 1 January 2027 it becomes before 1932 and a later reader must re-derive it. An 1849 London imprint clears the line by eighty-two years. This is a FOREIGN publication, so its United States term cannot be followed to its end from a domestic registration the way the 1843 Cummiskey's can; the age line is the whole of the case and is stated as such. Restoration under 17 U.S.C. 104A reaches only works still protected in the source country on 1 January 1996: Caswall died in 1878, so United Kingdom protection (life of the author plus seventy years) ended in 1948, and there was nothing left to restore. The basis is a United States one; a reader elsewhere must establish the position in their own jurisdiction.

THE SCAN AND ITS TEXT LAYER ADD NOTHING FOR ANYONE TO OWN. A faithful mechanical reproduction of a public-domain work is not original authorship (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., 36 F. Supp. 2d 191 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)), and machine optical character recognition adds no human authorship on top of it: the item's own metadata names the recogniser as ABBYY FineReader 11.0 (Extended OCR), an autonomous program and not a person.

AND THE GOOGLE MATTER WAS LOOKED FOR IN THESE BYTES RATHER THAN ASSUMED; SEE `notes`. Google's front-matter statement and usage guidelines are ABSENT from this file. What is present is the page-foot stamp alone, in 38 distinct spellings over 358 lines, carrying no notice and reserving nothing.

NOT RELIED ON, EXPRESSLY: that the Internet Archive item is available, that the download succeeded, or that the item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL -- it does, at `licenseurl`, and guidance/sources.md holds that host marks and successful downloads are insufficient. The 1849 book's own printed English is public domain independently of this digitisation.

artifacts.notes:
THE ARTIFACT THE ENGLISH WAS ACTUALLY READ FROM, in its per-leaf image form. The same images are served leaf by leaf at https://archive.org/download/LyraCatholica1849/page/n<leaf>_w1400.jpg, which is the route used here; those are renderings of these pages and not a separate acquisition.

LEAF RULE, DERIVED AND CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED: leaf = printed page + 37 through the body. Established at leaf n270, whose running head and folio read `FROM THE MISSAL. 233`, and held at every one of the twelve leaves opened between n270 and n281 and at all five between n175 and n179 (n175 = printed 138). It was not tested in the front matter or the indexes and must not be carried there.

LEAVES OPENED AND WHAT EACH CARRIES, all read at 1400 px width on 2026-08-19 and 2026-08-20: n8 the title leaf; n175 printed 138, the head `Friday after Passion-Sunday ... VESPERS. Stabat Mater dolorosa.` and its first three lines; n176-n179 printed 139-142, the Stabat Mater continued under MATINS and LAUDS to `Safe in Paradise with Thee.`; n270 printed 233, the end of the Good-Friday Crux fidelis and the head `Sequence, Easter-Sunday. Victimae Paschali laudes.`; n271 printed 234, the rest of it and the head `Sequence, Whit-Sunday. Veni Sancte Spiritus.`; n272-n273 printed 235-236, the rest of that and the head `Sequence, Solemnity of Corpus Christi. Lauda Sion Salvatorem.`; n274-n277 printed 237-240, the Lauda Sion entire, with the bracketed marker `[Ecce panis angelorum.]` standing at the head of its eleventh stanza on printed 240; n278 printed 241, the head `Sequence, Mass for the Dead. Dies irae dies illa.`; n279-n281 printed 242-244, the Dies irae entire, ending `Grant the Faithful light and rest.`, followed by `For Stabat Mater dolorosa, see page 138.` and `END OF HYMNS FROM THE MISSAL.`

QUALITY. The type is clean and unbroken at 1400 px and no line needed a second reading for its words. Two typographic details were not settled at that width and are recorded as open in the transcription artifact: the spacing around the two em dashes, and whether the printing sets a comma after `who died` in the third stanza of the Victimae paschali, where the text layer reads a full stop and the image reads a comma.

artifacts.notes:
One header line and 246 data lines. Columns: hymn, latin_incipit, printed_page, ia_leaf, stanza, line, english. `hymn` is one of victimae-paschali, veni-sancte-spiritus, lauda-sion, dies-irae, stabat-mater. `printed_page` and `ia_leaf` are the page and the zero-based Internet Archive leaf at which THAT LINE stands, so a strophe broken across a page break carries two different values and can be found at either.

COVERAGE: the five sequences the 1962 Missale Romanum appoints, entire, and nothing else from the book. Victimae Paschali laudes 6 stanzas / 19 lines; Veni Sancte Spiritus 10 stanzas / 30 lines; Lauda Sion Salvatorem 12 stanzas / 80 lines; Dies irae 19 stanzas / 57 lines; Stabat Mater dolorosa 10 stanzas / 60 lines.

STROPHE CORRESPONDENCE AGAINST THE LATIN THIS REPOSITORY CARRIES, counted, not assumed, on 2026-08-20 against src/sources/calendars/roman-1962/propers.yaml. Caswall sets the Latin's tercets two to a stanza and each of the five is complete strophe for strophe: Victimae paschali, 8 Latin strophes against 6 English stanzas, the fifth of which carries the two short strophes `Sepulcrum Christi viventis` and `Angelicos testes` together; Veni Sancte Spiritus, 10 against 10, one for one; Lauda Sion, 24 against 12, two for one throughout, with the Latin's two eight-line strophes (`Fracto demum` + `Nulla rei`) and its two closing ten-line strophes falling out as Caswall's eight- and ten-line stanzas; Dies irae, 19 against 19, one for one; Stabat Mater, 20 against 10, two for one throughout. NO CLAIM IS MADE HERE ABOUT FIDELITY OF WORDING. The count establishes that nothing is missing and nothing is added; whether a given English line renders its Latin well is an editorial judgement this file does not make.

WHAT THE ENGLISH DOES NOT RENDER. The 1962 Missal prints `Amen.` after the Stabat Mater and after the Dies irae, `Amen. Alleluja.` after the Victimae paschali, the Veni Sancte Spiritus and the Lauda Sion, and September's setting of the Stabat Mater ends `Amen. Alleluia.` Caswall prints none of these: the English simply ends. A consumer that needs the acclamation must supply it from the Latin proper and must not read its absence here as a variant reading.

TWO READINGS LEFT OPEN AT 1400 PX, both punctuation and neither affecting sense. The spacing around the em dash in `Heal our wounds — our strength renew;` (p. 235) and in `Signs, not things, are all we see;—` (p. 238) is transcribed as it appeared and was not re-read at a higher resolution; the two are recorded differently here because they appeared differently. And p. 234 line `The Prince of Life, who died,` is read with a comma on the image where the item's OCR reads a full stop; the image was preferred, per the rule that the text layer is a lead.

THE STABAT MATER IS TAKEN FROM THE BOOK'S OFFICE SECTION, ON THE BOOK'S OWN INSTRUCTION. Its Missal section prints, at p. 244, `For Stabat Mater dolorosa, see page 138.`, and p. 138 heads the text `Friday after Passion-Sunday ... VESPERS`, continuing under `MATINS (The same continued.)` at p. 140 and `LAUDS (The same continued.)` at p. 141. The three hours together are the twenty strophes of the Missal sequence with no doxology added at any break, and the closing stanza renders BOTH `Christe, cum sit hinc exire` and `Quando corpus morietur`, which is the Missal's ending; the eighteenth-century Breviary recension of this hymn ends otherwise. So this is the sequence and not a hymn cut down from it, and the cross-reference is the book's own.

work.author: Edward Caswall, M.A., translator
work.description: An English verse translation of the hymns of the Roman Breviary and of the hymns and sequences of the Roman Missal, with further hymns from the Paris and Cluny Breviaries and from the Italian Raccolta. Each piece is headed by the Latin incipit it renders and by the day or hour at which the book's source appoints it; the Latin itself is not printed beside the English. It is a devotional and literary collection, NOT a liturgical book: nothing in it was ever approved for use at the altar, and a reading taken from it attests what Caswall wrote, not what any Missal or Breviary printed. Caswall (1814-1878) made the translation as an Anglican clergyman received into the Catholic Church in 1847; he afterwards entered the Birmingham Oratory. The five sequences the Roman Missal appoints -- Victimae paschali laudes, Veni Sancte Spiritus, Lauda Sion Salvatorem, Dies irae, and Stabat Mater dolorosa -- are all in it, the first four together under a heading HYMNS FROM THE MISSAL and the Stabat Mater at the Friday after Passion Sunday, to which the Missal section cross-refers by page.
work.title: Lyra Catholica: containing all the Breviary and Missal hymns, with others from various sources
